| Xavier Dolan CMCQ |  
| --- |  
|  Dolan at the 2016 Cannes Film Festival |  
| Born | Xavier Dolan-Tadros 20 March 1989 (age 37) Montreal, Quebec, Canada |  
| Occupations | * Film director * producer * screenwriter * editor * actor * costume designer |  
| Years active | 1994–present |  
| Parent | Manuel Tadros (father) |  
| Awards | Full list |
**Xavier Dolan-Tadros**CMCQ (French:[[ɡzavje dɔlan tadʁɔs]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French");[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-1) born 20 March 1989) is a Canadian filmmaker and actor. He began his career as a child actor in commercials before directing several arthouse feature films. He first received international acclaim in 2009 for his feature film directorial debut, _I Killed My Mother_ (_J'ai tué ma mère_), which he also starred in, wrote, and produced, and which premiered at the 62nd Cannes Film Festival in the [Directors' Fortnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directors'_Fortnight "Directors' Fortnight") section and won three awards from the program.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-globe-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-mtlgaz-3)
Since 2009, he has written and directed eight feature films, all of which have premiered at Cannes, with the exception of _Tom at the Farm_—which premiered at the 70th Venice International Film Festival in 2013—and his first English-language film, _The Death & Life of John F. Donovan_, which premiered at the 2018 Toronto International Film Festival. Dolan has also directed music videos, notably with Adele for her singles "Hello" (2015), and "Easy on Me" (2021), for which he received a Grammy Award for Best Music Video nomination.
texts.1:
Dolan has won many accolades for his work, including the Jury Prize at the 2014 Cannes Film Festival for _Mommy_ and the Grand Prix at the 2016 Cannes Film Festival for _[It's Only the End of the World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's\_Only\_the\_End\_of\_the\_World "It's Only the End of the World")._ He has also won several Canadian Screen Awards and César Awards.
Outside of his own films, he has also starred in films from other directors, such as _Elephant Song_ (2014), _Boy Erased_ (2018), _Bad Times at the El Royale_ (2018), _It Chapter Two_ (2019), and _Lost Illusions_ (2021). He has received two nominations for the César Award for Best Supporting Actor; for _Lost Illusions_ in 2022 and _The Great Arch_ (2025) in 2026.
Dolan was born and raised in Montreal, Quebec.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-Bilefsky-4) He is the son of Geneviève Dolan, a Québécois public college administrator with Irish roots,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-Bilefsky-4) and Manuel Tadros, an Egyptian-Canadian actor and singer of Coptic and Lebanese descent.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-Mail-5) His parents divorced when he was 2 years old, leaving his mother to take care of him in suburban Montreal.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-:1-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-ctvnews-7) He has an older half-brother from his father's previous relationship.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-8)
texts.2:
He began acting at the age of 4, after his aunt, a production manager, suggested he auditioned for a minor role in a TV drama.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-anthem-9) Most notably he starred in a series of 21 commercials for a Canadian drugstore chain, Jean Coutu.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-10) He kept working until he was 8, when his mother, unable to cope with such a hyperactive child, sent him to boarding school in rural Quebec for 5 years.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-ctvnews-7)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-11)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-anthem-9)
His extensive dubbing career also started to intensify at this time, as Dolan found it hard to audition and get acting jobs. At first it was because he was away for school and then, when he was back in Montreal, because he was "too small, too big, too young, too old for all kinds of roles", according to casting directors.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-anthemmagazine-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-13) Once he completed his high school education, he decided to enroll at the College de Maisonneuve studying literature, but he will only last two months, later describing the experience as "suffocating".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-14)
Remembering his early days as an actor preceding his filmmaking debut, Dolan said:
texts.3:
> The director of a film I made when I was seven noticed I asked a lot of questions about everything. And he pointed at the director's chair and said: 'in 20 years, you're going to be sitting there.' But that wasn't clear to me at all. I wanted to be an actor. I became a director because I wanted to have the artistic authority to cast whoever I wanted in the lead role. I wrote my first film because I wanted to act again. I missed acting, I missed expressing things physically and emotionally.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-15)
Dolan attracted international attention with his directorial debut—a film about the complicated relationship between a mother and her teenage son—which he wrote, directed, produced and starred in at the age of 19.
He reportedly began writing the script when he was 16 years old.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-radiocanada-16) Talking about the genesis of the film, actress Anne Dorval, who starred as the titular mother and would later work on numerous projects with him, stated Dolan was only 15 when he first came to see her at her dubbing studio. The first script he gave her, _Pink Wings_ (_Les Ailes Roses_) was ultimately never filmed and it was described as "four films in one" by Dorval. As she turned him down, Dolan informed her he wasn't interested in that script anymore, and that he had decided to turn a short story he had written for French class, _The Matricide_ (_Le Matricide_),[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-17) into what would come to be known as _I Killed My Mother_ (_J'ai tué ma mère_).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-18)
He said in an interview with Canadian newspaper _Le Soleil_ that the film was partly autobiographical.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-lesoleil-19) When, years later, he was asked how his mother had received the film, he replied:
texts.4:
> I think it was easier for my mom to think it was just about somebody else. She said the only thing that woman and her had in common was that they were both stuck in traffic on a bridge every morning. Years later, we talked about it and she said, "When I saw the film, the first thing I said to myself was, I didn't know he hated me that much." But making that film, for me, was such an effort of modesty in terms of accepting what a brash, hysterical, egotistical kid I could have been and embracing the fact that I needed to be honest so the movie wouldn't be one-dimensional. Making that movie was all about making that woman a hero and the moments mocking her are so largely outnumbered by the moments glorifying her, while demonizing _him_–me. So for me, it was all about saying, "Didn't you know I _loved_ you that much?".[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-anthemmagazine-12)
Dolan at the 2009 Toronto International Film Festival
The film premiered at the [Director's Fortnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director's_Fortnight "Director's Fortnight") program of the 2009 Cannes Film Festival where it received an eight-minute standing ovation and won three awards: the Art Cinema Award, the SACD Prize for screenplay, and the Prix Regards Jeunes.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-Mail-5) It also won the Lumière Award for Best French-Language Film and four Jutra Awards, including Best Film, Best Screenplay, and Most Successful Film Outside Québec, beating out Denis Villeneuve's film _Polytechnique_ (2009) in what was deemed an "upset".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-20)
Dolan later said that the film was "flawed" and Peter Brunette of _The Hollywood Reporter_ called it "a somewhat uneven film that demonstrates a great deal of talent". Brunette also called the film "funny and audacious", while Allan Hunter of _Screen International_ said that it possessed "the sting of shrewdly observed truth".[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-canenc-21)
texts.5:
The film received the Claude Jutra Award (now known as the Canadian Screen Award for Best First Feature) at the Genies, and the Toronto Film Critics Association awarded Dolan the inaugural $5,000 Jay Scott Prize for emerging talent. _I Killed My Mother_ was named one of Canada's Top Ten features of the year by the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF) and chosen as Canada's official entry for Best Foreign Language Film for the 2010 Academy Awards, though it failed to receive a nomination from the academy.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-canenc-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-lacey-22) Distribution rights were later sold to more than 20 countries.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-hopewell-23) Due to legal problems experienced by the film's U.S. distributor, Regent Entertainment,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-24) it was not released theatrically in the U.S. until 2013, and once released, it earned little at the box office.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-:0-25)
The second feature film Dolan directed, _Heartbeats_ (_Les Amours imaginaires_), was financed privately.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-hopewell-23) The film follows two friends who are infatuated with the same mysterious young man and their friendship suffers. It premiered in the Un Certain Regard category at the 63e Festival de Cannes in May 2010 where it received a standing ovation.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-26) It won the top prize of the Official Competition at the Sydney Film Festival in June and screened at several film festivals throughout 2011, but failed to find audiences in non-French-speaking countries. It received several Genie nominations and the AQCC (Québec association of film critics) award for Best Film.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-canenc-21)
texts.6:
His third film, _Laurence Anyways_, was selected to compete in the _Un Certain Regard_ section at the 2012 Cannes Film Festival. Suzanne Clément's performance in the film won the section's award for Best Actress.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-Official_Selection-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-timescolonist-28) The film received praise or qualified praise from critics.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-30) A critic for MTV's _The Out Take_, which focuses on LGBT films, called the film "the best film of the year."[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-31) Despite the praise, the film was not released commercially for a year.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-32) Upon release, the film struggled at the box office,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-:0-25) and only grossed roughly $500,000 in Canada.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-33)
Dolan at the 2014 Cannes Film Festival
texts.7:
In May 2012, Dolan announced that his fourth film would be an adaptation of Michel Marc Bouchard's play _Tom at the Farm_ (_Tom à la ferme_).[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-34) It received its world premiere in the main competition section at the 70th Venice International Film Festival on 2 September 2013, and won the FIPRESCI award. Though _Tom at the Farm_ played the festival circuits in 2013, it was not released in the U.S. until 2015. In an August 2015 interview, Dolan said: "No one knows me in the States, because the movies have been released in such an awkward, irregular fashion, all by different distributors... I don't want to sound pretentious, but it's puzzling."[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-35)
Dolan's 2014 film, _Mommy_, shared the Jury Prize in the main competition section at the 2014 Cannes Film Festival with Jean-Luc Godard's film _Goodbye to Language_ (_Adieu au langage_).[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-36) The jury president for the 2014 festival was Jane Campion and, upon receiving the award, Dolan stated:
> _The Piano_ [Campion's film] was the first film that I watched that truly defined who I am... It made me want to write films for beautiful women with soul and will and strength. To even stand on the same stage as you [Campion] is extraordinary.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-37)
texts.8: The film was singled out by critics as Dolan's "most mature" film to date and proved to be a breakthrough in his career as a director.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-38) It was his first film to achieve significant success at the box office, grossing over $3.5 million domestically in 2014, becoming the highest-selling film in Quebec for 2014.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-kelly-39) According to the _Montreal Gazette_, over one million people watched it in France.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-kelly-39)_Mommy_ won the César Award for Best Foreign Film in 2015.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_Dolan#cite_note-40)

texts.0: Xavier Dolan (born Xavier Dolan-Tadros), CM, actor, director, writer, producer, editor, costume designer (born 20 March 1989 in Montreal, QC). A precocious practitioner of auteurist art cinema, Xavier Dolan garnered international acclaim at age 20 for his debut feature, _J’ai tué ma mère_(_I Killed My Mother_, 2009). His next four award-winning films — _Les amours imaginaires_(_Heartbeats_, 2010), _Laurence Anyways_ (2012), _Tom à la ferme_ (_Tom at the Farm_, 2013) and _Mommy_ (2014) — were completed by the time he was 25. His sixth movie, _Juste la fin du monde_ (_It’s Only the End of the World_, 2016), won the Grand Prix at the Cannes Film Festival and six Canadian Screen Awards. Dolan has also directed notable music videos for Adele and won a 2022 Juno Award for “Easy On Me.” He was made a Member of the Order of Canada in 2019.
texts.1:
### Early Years and Career
The son of schoolteacher Geneviève Dolan and actor and singer Manuel Tadros, Dolan began his acting career at age four. He appeared in television commercials, the television series _Omerta_ (1996) and _L’or_ (2001), and such films as Claude Fournier’s _J'en suis!_(1997), Roger Cantin’s _La forteresse suspendue_ (2001) and Pascal Laugier’s controversial horror movie _Martyrs_ (2008). He dropped out of school to pursue a career as an actor. He also found steady work dubbing French dialogue into films and TV series distributed in Quebec. He provided the voice of Stan in _South Park_, Ron Weasley in the _Harry Potter_ movies and Jacob Black in _Twilight Saga: New Moon_ (2009).
texts.2:
### J’ai tué ma mère (I Killed My Mother, 2009)
At age 17, Dolan wrote the script for his first feature film, _J’ai tué ma mère_(_I Killed My Mother_, 2009), which he planned to produce, direct and star in. He convinced Quebec TV star Anne Dorval to co-star and invested $150,000 of his own savings into the production. However, he ran out of money halfway through filming. After his distributor and producer backed out of the project, veteran production manager Carole Mondello came on board as executive producer. She helped Dolan complete the film by securing funds from the Quebec cultural development corporation, SODEC.
The semi-autobiographical film centres on a young gay teenager (Dolan) and his love-hate relationship with his mother (Dorval), who decides to send him to boarding school. The film received an eight-minute ovation following its premiere in the Directors’ Fortnight section at the Cannes Film Festival. Peter Brunette of the _Hollywood Reporter_ summed up the opinion of many critics — and even Dolan himself, who admitted the film was “flawed” — by calling it “a somewhat uneven film that demonstrates a great deal of talent.” Brunette also called the film “funny and audacious.” Allan Hunter of _Screen International_ said that it possessed “the sting of shrewdly observed truth.”
Video 13  
_J’ai tué ma mère_ won three prestigious awards at Cannes: the Art Cinema Award, the SACD Prize for screenplay and the Prix Regards Jeunes. It received more honours on the international festival circuit, including a Lumière Award as the best French film made outside France. It went on to receive four awards at the Prix Jutra (now the Prix Iris) including Best Screenplay, Most Successful Film Outside Québec and Best Film, upsetting Denis Villeneuve’s _Polytechnique_ (2009). However,_J’ai tué ma mère_ was shut out of all competitive categories at the Genie Awards. The film’s distributor, Louis Dussault of K-Films Amérique, labelled the Genies “totally irrelevant.”
texts.3:
### J’ai tué ma mère (I Killed My Mother, 2009)
The film did receive the Claude Jutra Award (now the Canadian Screen Award for Best First Feature) at the Genies. Dolan was also awarded the inaugural $5,000 Jay Scott Prize for emerging talent from the Toronto Film Critics Association. _J’ai tué ma mère_ was named one of Canada’s Top Ten features of the year by the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF). It was also chosen as Canada’s official entry for Best Foreign Language Film at the Academy Awards. However, due to legal problems experienced by the film’s US distributor, Regent Entertainment, it was not released theatrically in the United States until 2013.
Video 14
texts.4:
### Les amours imaginaires (Heartbeats, 2010)
Production of Dolan’s second film, _Les amours imaginaires_(_Heartbeats_) began in the fall of 2009. It was financed privately. Dolan wrote, directed, produced, edited and acted in the film. He also had a hand in the costumes and set design. The storyline follows two childhood friends, a young man and woman (Dolan and Maria Chokri), who fall in love with the same boy (Niels Schneider).
Imbued with a seductive musicality, the film won the Prix de la Jeunesse at Cannes and the top prize at the Sydney Film Festival. Back in Canada, it was nominated for four Genie Awards, including Best Motion Picture and Best Direction, and the AQCC (Québec association of film critics) award for best Quebec film. It was also named one of Canada’s Top Ten features of the year by TIFF.
texts.5:
### Laurence Anyways (2012)
Released in Quebec in May 2012, the much-anticipated _Laurence Anyways_ follows the decade-long journey of a transgender poet and literature professor (Melvil Poupaud) and the impact her transition has on her girlfriend (Suzanne Clément). Executive produced by American filmmaker Gus Vant Sant and made with a budget of just under $10 million, the stylistically bold film — alternately epic and inspired, messy and meandering — was selected to compete in the Un Certain Regard section of the Cannes Film Festival. It won the Queer Palm award and Clément was named Best Actress. It later received the Best Canadian Feature Film Award at TIFF — which also named it one of Canada’s Top Ten features of 2012 — as well as 11 Genie Award nominations and 11 nominations at the Prix Iris.
In March 2013, a retrospective of Dolan’s first three films were shown in New York as part of the Museum of Modern Art’s Canadian Front Series, an annual survey of Canadian films.
Video 15
texts.6:
### Tom à la ferme (Tom at the Farm, 2013)
Dolan’s fourth feature is an adaptation of Michel Marc Bouchard’s award-winning play _Tom à la ferme_. A sinister, Hitchcockian psychological thriller about a Montréal man (Dolan) who attends his dead lover’s funeral and is tormented by the deceased man’s brother (Pierre-Yves Cardinal), the film marked a rare move for Dolan into genre cinema. _Tom à la ferme_ premiered at the Venice Film Festival, where it received the FIPRESCI Prize. Shot by acclaimed cinematographer André Turpin (_Maelström_, _Incendies_), the visually inventive film plays with the aspect ratio in key sequences to enhance the suspense.
_Tom à la ferme_ was met with mixed reviews upon its theatrical release. It received nominations for eight Canadian Screen Awards, including Best Film, Direction and Adapted Screenplay, and was also named one of Canada’s Top Ten of the year by TIFF.
texts.7:
### Mommy (2014)
Dolan’s fifth feature, _Mommy_, essentially inverts the story of his first film. It is a sympathetic portrait of a middle-aged single mom (Dorval) who retrieves her violence-prone son (Antoine Olivier Pilon) from an institution and attempts to have him homeschooled by a neighbour (Clément). Like _Tom à la ferme_, _Mommy_ was shot by Turpin and again plays with the aspect ratio. The film is shot mostly in a 1:1 square frame, with certain scenes expanded to widescreen to mirror the expanding inner world of the characters.
_Mommy_ was met with a rapturous response following its premiere at the Cannes Film Festival, where the audience chanted “bravo!” over the end credits. It was favoured by many to win the Palme d’Or and ultimately tied for the Jury Prize with Jean-Luc Godard’s Adieu au langage (_Goodbye to Language 3D_, 2014).
_Mommy_ went on to become the most successful Canadian film of the year, sweeping both the Canadian Screen Awards and the Prix Iris. It won nine awards at each gala, including best film, director, editing and original screenplay at both. It also won the Prix Iris Billet d’or as the year’s highest-grossing film in Quebec, as well as the award for Most Successful Film outside Quebec. _Mommy_ grossed $3.3 million at the box office in Canada, netting it Telefilm Canada’s $40,000 Guichet d'or cash prize for the year’s highest-grossing French-language Canadian film.
Video 16
texts.8:
### Juste la fin du monde (It’s Only the End of the World, 2016)
Dolan adapted his next film, _Juste la fin du monde_ (_It’s Only the End of the World_, 2016), from the play of the same name by acclaimed French playwright Jean-Luc Lagarce. It is Dolan’s first film set outside Canada. It tells the story of a famous playwright who returns to his hometown after a long absence to tell his family he is dying.
Featuring a star-studded French cast including Gaspard Ulliel, Nathalie Baye, Léa Seydoux, Vincent Cassel and Marion Cotillard, the film won the Grand Prix and the Prize of the Ecumenical Jury at the Cannes Film Festival — the first Canadian film to do so since Atom Egoyan’s _The Sweet Hereafter_ (1997). However, _Juste la fin du monde_ was considered a controversial winner of the Grand Prix, the festival’s second-place award, since it received largely negative reviews from critics. Jon Frosch of the _Hollywood Reporter_ called the film “cold and deeply unsatisfying… a disappointment, even for the Dolan faithful.” _Time Out_’s Catherine Bray called it Dolan’s “worst by some distance, a talky unsatisfying anticlimax,” and wrote that the “wonderful cast [is] sadly wasted on a screeching melodrama.”
However, the film did have its champions. The _Guardian_’s Peter Bradshaw called it “histrionic and claustrophobic: deliberately oppressive and pretty well pop-eyed in its madness — and yet a brilliant, stylised and hallucinatory evocation of family dysfunction.” _Variety_’s Peter Debruge seemed to straddle both camps, calling the film “a frequently excruciating dramatic experience in which characters seem almost never to stop talking.” He also noted that “there is a welcome maturity to _It’s Only the End of the World_ that was absent in [Dolan’s] five previous features — and also a rare restraint.”
_Juste la fin du monde_ went on to win César Awards (the French equivalent of the Oscar) for Best Director and Best Editing, as well as six Canadian Screen Awards, including for Best Director and Best Motion Picture.
Video 17
texts.9:
### The Death and Life of John F. Donovan (2016)
Dolan began prepping his first English-language feature, _The Death and Life of John F. Donovan,_ in July 2014. The script, co-written with Jacob Tierney (_The Trotsky_, _Letterkenny_), focuses on a pen pal relationship between a young boy and a Hollywood movie star. The idea was inspired by a letter Dolan wrote to Leonardo DiCaprio as an eight-year-old.
The film, which stars Kit Harington, Natalie Portman, Jacob Tremblay, Susan Sarandon and Kathy Bates, had a troubled production. Dolan spent two years editing the film and turned down two invitations to premiere it at the Cannes Film Festival. After the first cut of the film clocked in at more than four hours, Dolan cut an entire subplot featuring Jessica Chastain.
When the film finally premiered at TIFF in 2018, critical opinion was mixed at best. _Variety_’s Peter Debruge called it “A work of stunning technique eclipsed by its increasingly jaw-dropping solipsism.” The _Guardian_’s Benjamin Lee called it “a film so befuddling to watch and understand that one can sense the tortured post-production process lingering over every scene.” The _AV Club_’s Mike D’Angelo called it “a barely coherent upchuck of raw emotion.” _The Death and Life of John F. Donovan_ was released in December 2019 to mostly negative reviews, scoring 28/100 on the aggregator _Metacritic_.
Video 18
texts.10:
### Matthias & Maxime (2019)
Dolan’s next film, _Matthias & Maxime_, saw him return to more familiar ground. It looks at the effects that a single kiss — staged for a film — between two male friends (played by Dolan and Gabriel D’Almeida Freitas) has on their friendship and their conceptions of self. _NOW_ magazine’s Kevin Ritchie called it Dolan’s “most engaging and modest film in years… a solid rebound for Dolan in the wake of his obnoxiously self-righteous English-language debut, _The Death And Life Of John F. Donovan_.” The _Guardian_’s Peter Bradshaw called it an “unstoppably garrulous, sweet-natured” film that is filled with “tenderness and gentleness.”
texts.11:
### Characteristic Traits
The _Montreal Gazette_’s Brendan Kelly has described Dolan’s movies as “very personal films that mix melodrama, stylish visual direction and art-film smarts.” _Out_ magazine’s Adam Rathe has observed that all of Dolan’s films portray “characters tangled up in provocative, erotically charged plotlines.” Indeed, the idea of impossible love is a recurring theme in his films. In an interview with the _Huffington Post_, Dolan stated that his films delve into “the whole process of humiliation by love.”
Although he has been held up as a champion of queer cinema, Dolan has rejected the title, stating, “There’s no such thing as queer cinema. My generation has sexual, sensual and sentimental boundaries that are completely different from those of the generations that precede us… I’ve never been coy about or ashamed of being gay, but I’ve been making a relentless effort, since the first scene of _I Killed My Mother_, to avoid claiming things. These movies are not fights for rights, they’re movies.”
Dolan has built a reputation for being obsessive about virtually every onscreen detail of his films. In addition to being the writer, director, producer and editor, he also designs the costumes and meticulously oversees the art direction and music selection. “The control of every detail is my guarantee of accessing the type of material I’m satisfied with,” he has said. He has even claimed that the trailer for _Laurence Anyways_ is, frame by frame, exactly as he visualized it before he wrote the screenplay.
texts.12:
### Music Videos
In 2013, Dolan’s music video for the song “College Boy” by French new wave band Indochine sparked international controversy for its violent imagery, which includes the beating, shooting and crucifixion of a gay teenager (played by _Mommy_’s Antoine Olivier Pilon). The video was banned by Quebec’s MusiquePlus, and censored on YouTube and in France. Dolan wrote an open letter for the _Huffington Post_ defending the video, and was quoted in interviews saying, “It seems absurd to me that this video is censored. Is it really more violent than all the films arriving on our screens every day?”
Dolan also directed and edited the music video for Adele’s hit song “Hello,” released in October 2015 as the lead single for her album _25_. The first music video shot using IMAX cameras, “Hello” was viewed 50 million times on YouTube in the first 48 hours and became the fastest video to reach 1 billion views on YouTube, doing so in less than three months.
In 2021, Dolan directed an advertising campaign for Chopard watches and jewelry starring Julia Roberts. He also directed the music video for “Easy On Me,” the lead single for Adele’s album _30_. Filmed in Quebec’s Eastern Townships, the video amassed more than 275 million views in seven months and went on to win the 2022 Juno Award for Music Video of the Year.
texts.13:
### Other Projects
Xavier Dolan narrated the Genie Award-winning short documentary _Lipsett Diaries_ (2010), an animated NFB film about experimental filmmaker Arthur Lipsett. Dolan continued to dub French dialogue into numerous Hollywood films, including _How to Train Your Dragon_ (2010), _Kick-Ass_ (2010), _John Carter_ (2012) and _The Hunger Games_ (2012). He co-starred in Daniel Grou’s _Miraculum_ (2014) and Charles Binamé’s English-language feature _Elephant Song_ (2014), co-starring Bruce Greenwood, Catherine Keener and Carrie-Anne Moss. He also appeared in _Boy Erased_ (2018), _Bad Times at the El Royale_ (2018), _It Chapter Two_(2019), and the acclaimed French film _Illusions perdues_ (2021), which won the César Award for Best Film and earned Dolan a César nomination for Best Supporting Actor.

**Jason R. Reitman** (; born October 19, 1977)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-up-in-the-air-bio-1) is a Canadian and American filmmaker. He is best known for directing the films _Thank You for Smoking_ (2005), _Juno_ (2007), _Up in the Air_ (2009), _Young Adult_ (2011), _Ghostbusters: Afterlife_ (2021), and _Saturday Night_ (2024). He has received a Grammy Award, a Golden Globe, and four Academy Award nominations, two for Best Director. He is the son of director Ivan Reitman and is known for frequently collaborating with screenwriter Diablo Cody and director Gil Kenan.
Reitman was born in Montreal, Quebec,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-up-in-the-air-bio-1) the son of Geneviève Robert, an actress sometimes billed as Geneviève Deloir, and film director Ivan Reitman (1946–2022). He has two younger sisters: Catherine Reitman, an actress, producer and writer, who is four years younger, and Caroline Reitman, a nurse, who is 11 years younger.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-WTF-Maron-2014-2)
texts.1:
Jason Reitman's father was born in Czechoslovakia, to Jewish parents who were Holocaust survivors. His paternal grandfather ran a dry cleaner and then a car wash.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-WTF-Maron-2014-2) His mother is of French-Canadian descent and grew up a Christian; she converted to Judaism.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-ref101-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-BayAreaReporter-Up-2009-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-jpost-696496-5) When he was still a child, his family moved to Los Angeles.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-6) His father, Ivan, directed the films _Ghostbusters_, _Ghostbusters II_, _Stripes_, and _Kindergarten Cop_.
Jason Reitman grew up on sets and has photos of himself as a baby on the set of _Animal House_ in 1978;[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-WTF-Maron-2014-2)Bill Murray said that Reitman was "a pain in the ass" while filming _Ghostbusters_, with Dan Aykroyd joking that "he was directing back then".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-yt20211115-7) Such experiences showed him that making movies is "a job that people do, that it's not just this piece of magic that happens".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-WTF-Maron-2014-2) Reitman made a cameos in a few of his father's films, notably in _Kindergarten Cop_ in which he played a student at the school who is caught making out with a girl by John Kimble, who is played by Arnold Schwarzenegger.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-8)
texts.2:
Reitman feels he was "a loser... a movie geek...[and] shy" as a child.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-RobertEbert-Juno-2007-9) In the late 1980s, he began appearing in small acting parts and serving as a production assistant on his father's films. He learned how to edit film in the editing rooms of his father's movies.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-RobertEbert-Juno-2007-9) Reitman graduated from Harvard-Westlake School in Studio City, Los Angeles in 1995. He was a high jumper in high school, coached by Occidental College Hall-of-Famer Phil Sweeney.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-10)
Reitman attended Skidmore College in Saratoga Springs, New York and was to major in pre-med studies before transferring to the University of Southern California (USC) in Los Angeles to major in English and creative writing. At USC, he performed with improv group Commedus Interruptus.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-DailyTrojan-UpAir-2009-11)
Reitman began making short films while at USC.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-WTF-Maron-2014-2) Throughout his 20s, instead of accepting offers to make commercial feature films, he made his own short films and directing commercials. Although he was offered the opportunity to direct _[Dude, Where's My Car?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dude,\_Where's\_My\_Car%3F "Dude, Where's My Car?")_ on two occasions, he declined.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-RobertEbert-Juno-2007-9)
Reitman in 2007
texts.3:
Reitman's first feature film, _Thank You for Smoking_, opened in 2005. Reitman developed the Christopher Buckley novel into a screenplay and, eventually, a film. The film was a commercial and critical success. It grossed over $39 million worldwide by the end of its run, and was nominated for two Golden Globes. After the success of _Thank You for Smoking_, Reitman mentioned in an interview that his next film would be adapting another book (a "white collar satire") into a film. He also mentioned that he had plans to work with Buckley again on an original project.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-ignore-12) Although the first of the projects eventually became _Up in the Air_, the second project has not come to fruition.
His second film, _Juno_, generated great buzz after it premiered at the 2007 Toronto International Film Festival[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-Evans2007-13) and was released in December 2007. It was Roger Ebert's favorite film of 2007 and received Oscar nominations for Best Picture, Elliot Page's performance as the title character, Diablo Cody's original screenplay, and Reitman himself for Best Director. Reitman did win other awards for his work on _Juno_, including Best Director at the 2008 Canadian Comedy Awards. The film grossed over $140 million at the U.S. box office, making it the largest success of Reitman's career and more successful than any of his father's films since _Kindergarten Cop_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-14)Brad Silberling was originally attached to direct the film, but he dropped out over casting differences.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-15) Reitman was in the middle of writing a screenplay when he came on board to direct _Juno_ and, at one point, he expressed intent to finish writing and to direct this screenplay.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-16)
texts.4:
In March 2006, Reitman formed the production company "Hard C Productions" with producing partner Daniel Dubiecki. The company had an overall deal with Fox Searchlight Pictures, the company that distributed Reitman's first two films. Reitman described his production company's goal as being to produce "small subversive comedy that is independent but accessible".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-bonzai-17) Reitman states that he and Dubiecki "want to make unusual films, and anything that turns a genre on its ear".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-jennifer-18) Through Hard C Productions, Reitman is set to produce and direct _Banzai Shadowhands_, a comedy about "a once-great ninja who is now living a life of mediocrity". _Shadowhands_ will be written by _The Office'_ s Rainn Wilson. Reitman met Wilson on the set of his father's film _My Super Ex-Girlfriend_, in which Wilson had a supporting role.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-bonzai-17) No start date for filming has been set, and it is unclear as to whether or not Wilson is finished with the script.
Hard C Productions produced films _The Ornate Anatomy of Living Things_ and _[Jennifer's Body](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer's\_Body "Jennifer's Body")_. _Anatomy_ has been written by Matthew Spicer and Max Winkler, and will revolve around "a Gotham bookstore clerk who discovers a museum devoted to his life".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-19)_Jennifer's Body_ is a horror comedy written by Diablo Cody and starring Megan Fox, about a cheerleader who is possessed by a demon and starts feeding off the boys in a Minnesota farming town.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-jennifer-18) In 2009, Reitman left Hard C to form Right of Way Films.
texts.5:
In 2001, the year the novel _Up in the Air_ was published, Sheldon Turner discovered the book and wrote a screenplay adaptation, which he sold to DreamWorks in 2003. Jason Reitman later came upon the novel (initially attracted by the Christopher Buckleyblurb on the cover) while browsing in the Los Angeles bookstore Book Soup.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-VR1118012459-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-wrap012510-21) Reitman persuaded his father Ivan Reitman to purchase the book's film rights, and the elder Reitman commissioned a screenplay from Ted and Nicholas Griffin, who used some elements from Turner's script in their own work. Jason Reitman then developed his own screenplay, incorporating some of the elements from the Griffins' script that had (unbeknownst to Reitman) originated with Turner. Some of Turner's inventions that were utilized in the final film include Ryan's boilerplate termination speech ("Anyone who ever built an empire or changed the world sat where you're sitting right now..."), a key plot point involving a suicide, and the character of Ryan's partner (written by Turner as male).[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-wrap012510-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-LAT_2010-01-15-22)
Reitman at the 2009 Toronto International Film Festival
Reitman initially attempted to claim sole credit for writing the film, and later admitted to being confused when the Writers Guild of America ruled that he should share credit with Turner. He and Turner later appeared at a WGA event where both said they were happy to share credit now that the course of events, and Turner's contribution to the final product, had been made clear.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-wrap012510-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-LAT_2010-01-15-22)
texts.6: In the spring of 2009, Reitman directed _Up in the Air_ starring George Clooney. _Up in the Air_ is based on a novel written by Walter Kirn about a corporate downsizer who travels from city to city and is fanatical about collecting his ten millionth frequent flier mile. The film features real-world characters cast from the ranks of the recently downsized. "Hidden within a film that seems to be about corporate termination and the economy is a movie about the decision whether to be alone or not," noted Reitman,"[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-23) in an interview conducted just prior to the film's nationwide release. Sheldon Turner and Reitman's _Up in the Air_ screenplay won the Golden Globe Award for best screenplay in 2010.
texts.7: Reitman was also an executive producer of the erotic thriller _Chloe_, theatrically released by Sony Pictures Classics on March 26, 2010.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-boxofficemojo.com-24) Reitman helped persuade Amanda Seyfried to star in the film.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-25) The film enjoyed commercial success and became director Atom Egoyan's biggest moneymaker ever.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-26) On January 15, 2019, Reitman announced he would be working on _Ghostbusters: Afterlife_, a continuation of the original _Ghostbusters_ films directed by his father.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-28) Originally set for a June 2021, release, due to the COVID-19 pandemic the release date was pushed back to November 11, 2021.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-29) After the success of the film, both Reitman and his _Ghostbusters: Afterlife_ co-writer and collaborator Gil Kenan formed their own production company Reitman/Kenan Productions and had signed an overall deal with Sony Pictures Entertainment to develop more projects.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-30) Reitman was set to return to direct the sequel to _Ghostbusters: Afterlife_ entitled _Frozen Empire_, but later was replaced by Kenan, who remains as a producer and co-writer in the film, was released in 2024.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-31)
texts.8:
On October 11, 2024, Reitman directed and co-wrote alongside Kenan _Saturday Night_, a comedy biopic about the events directly preceding the live broadcast of _Saturday Night Live_'s first episode on October 11, 1975. Canadian comedian Dan Aykroyd was a member of that _SNL_ cast and describes the film as a "stand alone masterpiece."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-32)
Reitman in 2012
Before his feature film career began, Jason Reitman wrote and directed six short films. He financed his first short film, _Operation_, with money he made by selling ads in desk calendars. The film premiered at the Sundance Film Festival in 1998.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman#cite_note-advocates-33) He was a guest on _The Howard Stern Show_ on April 10, 2008; when he was asked if he would direct _Ghostbusters III_ and cast Howard, he said: "Do you know how many times I get asked if I want to do _Ghostbusters III_? Looking at my career so far, I mean, if you just looked at my two films, I would make the most boring _Ghostbusters_ movie. It would just be people talking about ghosts, there wouldn't be any ghost-busting in it." Stern, a friend of Ivan Reitman, also revealed that he had seen Jason's early short films and was impressed enough to offer him the opportunity to direct an episode of _Son of the Beach_ (a TV series he produced, a goofy parody of _Baywatch_), which Jason declined, citing that he was busy obtaining financing for _Thank You for Smoking_ at the time.

4.9M This 31-second reel tells the story of a man who refused to sell his house despite it being in the direct path of a new road project. Authorities reportedly offered him over $200,000, but he declined, leading engineers to construct the road around his property instead. The setup included a concrete tunnel as the only access point to his home, isolating it from direct entry. While the decision drew attention for its defiance, constant traffic noise and vibrations from passing vehicles eventually made living conditions difficult. The situation highlights how personal choices can conflict with large-scale infrastructure development and long-term practicality.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Apollo 7 astronaut Walt Cunningham in 1968
As of 2026, thirty United States astronauts have graduated from the University of California (UC) system, including 10 from UC Berkeley, 10 from UCLA, 4 from UC San Diego, 3 from UC Santa Barbara, 2 from UC Davis, 1 from UC Irvine, and 1 from UC Santa Cruz.
The first alumnus to fly as an astronaut was Walt Cunningham (UCLA), selected in 1963 in NASA Astronaut Group 3 to fly as the Lunar Module Pilot on Apollo 7, the first Apollo Program mission. As of 2026, the most recent alumna to be selected as an astronaut was Deniz Burnham (UC San Diego), of the class of 2021. One alumnus was part of the Apollo program, three were part of Soyuz, and twenty were part of the Space Shuttle program. In total, 31 people educated at the University of California campuses have flown to space, either for NASA or through private space companies.
The UC system is the flagshipland-grantpublic university system in the U.S. state of California. The first campus was established at Berkeley in 1868, followed by Los Angeles in 1919 and major expansion in the 1960s to San Diego, Irvine, and Santa Cruz. The system includes 9 undergraduate campuses in total, including at Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, Merced, Riverside, San Diego, Santa Barbara, and Santa Cruz.
In addition to the 30 astronauts who are alumni of the University of California, the university system has produced 670 Olympic medalists, 254 members of the National Academy of Sciences, and 75 Nobel Prize laureates.

## University of California, Berkeley

Alumni of the University of California, Berkeley include 10 NASA astronauts and 1 private astronaut.

#### Distinguished Educator in Residence, Emeritus, at Boise State University
Barbara Morgan is an educator and retired NASA astronaut. Morgan is the public elementary
school teacher who trained with the Challenger crew as the back-up for Teacher in Space
Christa McAuliffe, then later served as a NASA astronaut for 10 years.
Morgan graduated with honors and a bachelor’s degree in Human Biology from Stanford
University. She earned her teaching credential at College of Notre Dame (Notre Dame de
Namur University). She taught public school for 24 years in diverse locations including the Bay
Area in California, the Flathead Indian Reservation in Montana, a small mountain town in Idaho,
and Colegio Americano in Quito, Ecuador. In 1985, Morgan (back-up) and Christa McAuliffe
(Teacher in Space) were selected to train with the space shuttle Challenger crew. After that
mission ended tragically shortly after lift-off with the loss of the crew, NASA asked Morgan to
continue as Teacher in Space Designee. She returned to her teaching in Idaho and continued to
work for NASA, part-time, where her duties included public speaking, educational consulting,
curriculum design, and serving on the National Science Foundation’s Task Force for Women and
Minorities in Science and Engineering.
NASA selected Morgan to the 1998 astronaut class. She flew 5.3 million miles in space in 2007
on STS-118, a two-week mission to help construct the International Space Station. Her duties
included operating the space shuttle and space station robotic arms, serving as loadmaster,
assisting the pilots with re-entry and landing, and teaching lessons from orbit to schoolchildren
on Earth. In addition to spaceflight, Morgan worked in Mission Control as prime communicator
(“Capcom”) with on-orbit crews, and she served in the Space Station Operations Branch and
Robotics Branch of the Astronaut Office.
Morgan retired from NASA in 2008 to become Distinguished Educator in Residence at Boise
State University, where she represented the university and provided vision and leadership to
the State of Idaho, primarily in STEM education. Her work included policy and program
development, advocacy, and mentoring. Currently, Morgan works with Boise State University as
Emeritus, and continues to work with national and international education organizations, other
non-profits, and NASA.

#### Distinguished Educator in Residence, Emeritus, at Boise State University
Morgan’s many awards include, most recently, the Columbia University Teachers College Medal
for Distinguished Service and the inaugural Idaho Medal of Achievement, the state’s highest
civilian honor for service. She has earned two honorary doctorates ‒ in science and public
service ‒ and has two public schools named after her.

Ellison Onizuka became the first Asian American astronaut in 1985 on the Space Shuttle Challenger. Raised in rural Hawaii, Ellison showed that with determination and hard work, anyone can achieve their dreams. He graduated from the University of Colorado with bachelor's and master's degrees in aerospace engineering.
Before becoming an astronaut, he was an engineer and pilot in the U.S. Air Force. After that, he joined NASA's astronaut program and went through a lot of training for space missions. He learned how to operate spacecraft, perform spacewalks, and conduct scientific experiments in space. He also studied survival skills for emergencies and worked closely with other astronauts to prepare for their missions.
Onizuka was selected by NASA in 1978 and flew his first mission aboard the Challenger in January 1985. His contributions to space exploration paved the way for future generations of diverse astronauts.
Tragically Onizuka perished in the Challenger disaster in 1986, along with six other crew members when the shuttle exploded shortly after launch. He lost his life in the Challenger disaster but his legacy continues to inspire many.
Onizuka's legacy has been honored through several recognitions, including schools and programs named after him. His name stands out among other space pioneers like Neil Armstrong, showing the contributions and sacrifices made by many different people in the quest for space exploration.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Apollo 7 astronaut Walt Cunningham in 1968
As of 2026, thirty United States astronauts have graduated from the University of California (UC) system, including 10 from UC Berkeley, 10 from UCLA, 4 from UC San Diego, 3 from UC Santa Barbara, 2 from UC Davis, 1 from UC Irvine, and 1 from UC Santa Cruz.
The first alumnus to fly as an astronaut was Walt Cunningham (UCLA), selected in 1963 in NASA Astronaut Group 3 to fly as the Lunar Module Pilot on Apollo 7, the first Apollo Program mission. As of 2026, the most recent alumna to be selected as an astronaut was Deniz Burnham (UC San Diego), of the class of 2021. One alumnus was part of the Apollo program, three were part of Soyuz, and twenty were part of the Space Shuttle program. In total, 31 people educated at the University of California campuses have flown to space, either for NASA or through private space companies.
The UC system is the flagshipland-grantpublic university system in the U.S. state of California. The first campus was established at Berkeley in 1868, followed by Los Angeles in 1919 and major expansion in the 1960s to San Diego, Irvine, and Santa Cruz. The system includes 9 undergraduate campuses in total, including at Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, Merced, Riverside, San Diego, Santa Barbara, and Santa Cruz.
In addition to the 30 astronauts who are alumni of the University of California, the university system has produced 670 Olympic medalists, 254 members of the National Academy of Sciences, and 75 Nobel Prize laureates.

## [Blount and Beyond](https://www.facebook.com/groups/1774040246167748/?__cft__[0]=AZhE9prwyvUWajQv4RPeeqEKdblgJmIkHrhOIVHILt1pzA1FM4b1v1o5wb8e4VL51FngD83H8XG-w6DRzp-3S-yCudZxGWPz4nL2hBH2DG687_OU9fv6TnfvtgaK4elvm20EaN3ZX95M4bjEkJwDGMCcpMBuRnY2HKGWK6_o--qFBJXxPWncIio7&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R) ·
Ellison Onizuka became the first Asian American astronaut in 1985 on the Space Shuttle Challenger. Raised in rural Hawaii, Ellison showed that with determination and hard work, anyone can achieve their dreams. He graduated from the University of Colorado with bachelor's and master's degrees in aerospace engineering.
Before becoming an astronaut, he was an engineer and pilot in the U.S. Air Force. After that, he joined NASA's astronaut program and went through a lot of training for space missions. He learned how to operate spacecraft, perform spacewalks, and conduct scientific experiments in space. He also studied survival skills for emergencies and worked closely with other astronauts to prepare for their missions.
Onizuka was selected by NASA in 1978 and flew his first mission aboard the Challenger in January 1985. His contributions to space exploration paved the way for future generations of diverse astronauts.
Tragically Onizuka perished in the Challenger disaster in 1986, along with six other crew members when the shuttle exploded shortly after launch. He lost his life in the Challenger disaster but his legacy continues to inspire many.
Onizuka's legacy has been honored through several recognitions, including schools and programs named after him. His name stands out among other space pioneers like Neil Armstrong, showing the contributions and sacrifices made by many different people in the quest for space exploration.

William Kesling, Designer/Builder | The Atol Residence, 1938

You enter the house and immediately meet one of its strongest moments: a corner window framing the view.

It is an early version of the modern corner-glass condition — not yet the seamless butt-glazed detail that would become common later, but a carefully composed industrial-style window system with structure still required at the corner.

The proportions are equally deliberate. The glazing follows a repeating rule of three, both vertically and horizontally, giving the elevation a clear rhythm.

Kesling’s Los Angeles career was remarkably brief but productive. Beginning in the mid-1930s, he completed a concentrated body of work before legal and financial troubles effectively ended his design-build practice in the city. The Atol Residence was completed at the end of that short period, making it an especially compelling document of his work.

Architecture, construction, cost, and ambition were already colliding in the 1930s — some things have not changed very much.

[FROM THE ARCHIVE Raphael Soriano, FAIA, Architect El Paradiso, 1964 Also known as the Grossman House Renovation by Linda Brettler, AIA El Paradiso is especially significant within Raphael Soriano’s body of work as the only surviving all-aluminum residence he designed. The structural system is remarkably direct: slender 3-by-3-inch aluminum columns support paired C-channels above, with exposed fasteners making the method of assembly legible throughout the house. A lightweight corrugated aluminum roof deck continues the logic, while floor-to-ceiling aluminum sliders reduce the boundary between enclosure and landscape. That transparency is one of the reasons the house feels considerably larger than its roughly 3,800 square feet. Views extend through the interior toward the pool and hillside, while outdoor spaces function almost as additional rooms—including an exterior living area organized around a fire pit. Soriano’s planning is equally disciplined. Full-height storage is concealed behind continuous floor-to-ceiling doors, allowing entire walls to function as closets while preserving the visual calm of the interior. Storage, structure, glazing, and circulation are all integrated into the architecture rather than treated as separate elements. Perched on a narrow hillside lot above Studio City, the house was later thoughtfully revived by architect Linda Brettler. Working from Soriano’s original drawings, Brettler restored the clarity of the 1964 design while correcting decades of mismatched alterations. A compelling example of how lightweight structure, transparency, built-in storage, and a close relationship to landscape can make a relatively modest footprint feel expansive. # FROM THE ARCHIVE William Kesling, Designer/Builder | The Atol Residence, 1938 You enter the house and immediately meet one of its strongest moments: a corner window framing the view. It is an early version of the modern corner-glass condition — not yet the seamless butt-glazed detail that would become common later, but a carefully composed industrial-style window system with structure still required at the corner. The proportions are equally deliberate. The glazing follows a repeating rule of three, both vertically and horizontally, giving the elevation a clear rhythm. Kesling’s Los Angeles career was remarkably brief but productive. Beginning in the mid-1930s, he completed a concentrated body of work before legal and financial troubles effectively ended his design-build practice in the city. The Atol Residence was completed at the end of that short period, making it an especially compelling document of his work. Architecture, construction, cost, and ambition were already colliding in the 1930s — some things have not changed very much. [FROM THE ARCHIVE Raphael Soriano, FAIA, Architect El Paradiso, 1964 Also known as the Grossman House Renovation by Linda Brettler, AIA El Paradiso is especially significant within Raphael Soriano’s body of work as the only surviving all-aluminum residence he designed. The structural system is remarkably direct: slender 3-by-3-inch aluminum columns support paired C-channels above, with exposed fasteners making the method of assembly legible throughout the house. A lightweight corrugated aluminum roof deck continues the logic, while floor-to-ceiling aluminum sliders reduce the boundary between enclosure and landscape. That transparency is one of the reasons the house feels considerably larger than its roughly 3,800 square feet. Views extend through the interior toward the pool and hillside, while outdoor spaces function almost as additional rooms—including an exterior living area organized around a fire pit. Soriano’s planning is equally disciplined. Full-height storage is concealed behind continuous floor-to-ceiling doors, allowing entire walls to function as closets while preserving the visual calm of the interior. Storage, structure, glazing, and circulation are all integrated into the architecture rather than treated as separate elements. Perched on a narrow hillside lot above Studio City, the house was later thoughtfully revived by architect Linda Brettler. Working from Soriano’s original drawings, Brettler restored the clarity of the 1964 design while correcting decades of mismatched alterations. A compelling example of how lightweight structure, transparency, built-in storage, and a close relationship to landscape can make a relatively modest footprint feel expansive. Beautifully shot by Orlando Hernandez Orlando Hernandez THE VALUE OF ARCHITECTURE Properties With Design Integrity.

[[](https://www.instagram.com/insidehistory) insidehistory 1.6M Construction work in the 1980s operated at a level of danger that feels almost unbelievable today! 😳 Back then, American high-rise crews routinely walked across open steel beams hundreds of feet in the air with nothing but a tool belt and raw instinct. Safety rules technically existed, but enforcement varied widely, and job-site culture mattered just as much. Many workers felt harnesses slowed them down, and companies often prioritized speed and cost over strict protection standards.
